start.title: Start here: your Terraform path
start.description: You can package an app (Docker), run it (Kubernetes), and install it with one command (Helm). But where do the servers, networks, and the cluster itself…
start.html:
You can package an app (Docker), run it (Kubernetes), and install it with one command (Helm). But where do the servers, networks, and the cluster itself come from? Terraform builds them from files you write.

The big idea
Write down the infrastructure you want. Terraform compares it with what exists, shows you a plan, and makes only the changes you approve.

Before starting: nothing is required. Knowing what a server and a network are helps. No installation or cloud account is needed until the final stage, and even then everything runs on your own computer for free.

1 · Meet Terraform · lessons 1–3Explain infrastructure as code and where Terraform fits next to Docker, Kubernetes, and Helm.
2 · Write and apply · lessons 4–7Read a configuration, run init → plan → apply in the simulator, and learn what the state file remembers.
3 · Change safely · lessons 8–11Read plan symbols, catch drift, reuse code with modules, and fix common errors.
4 · Use it for real · lessons 12–14Learn team habits, then run a real project on your computer and complete the final mission.

Use Explore Terraform for free practice at any time. Your Terraform progress is saved separately from the other topics.

idea.title: Infrastructure as code: write what you want
idea.description: Your 🍕 app needs a server, a storage bucket for menu photos, and a web address. You click through a cloud website to create them. Six months later you need…
idea.html:
The problem
Your 🍕 app needs a server, a storage bucket for menu photos, and a web address. You click through a cloud website to create them. Six months later you need the same setup for testing. Which buttons did you click? Which settings did you choose? Nobody remembers.
The big idea
Describe your infrastructure in text files. Terraform reads them and makes the real world match. The files become the single source of truth: you can review them, keep them in git, and run them again.
Think of it like…
A recipe versus cooking from memory. With a recipe anyone can make the same pizza again, and you can see exactly what changed between versions.

Three words to know

WordMeaning
ResourceOne thing Terraform manages: a server, a bucket, a DNS record, even a file.
ProviderA plugin that knows how to talk to one platform: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, GitHub, and thousands more.
PlanA preview of exactly what Terraform will add, change, or destroy before it touches anything.

Terraform is declarative: you write the end result (“one small server in eu-west”), not the steps (“click Create, choose a size…”). Kubernetes works the same way: you describe the desired state, and something else does the work.

Remember
  • Infrastructure as code means infrastructure described in files you can review and repeat.
  • Providers talk to platforms; resources are the things they create.
  • Always read the plan before you approve it.

quiz.q: Why write infrastructure in files instead of clicking in a web console?
options: Files can be reviewed, repeated, and kept in git
quiz.why: The big win is a repeatable, reviewable record of what should exist.

quiz.q: What is a provider?
options: A plugin that lets Terraform talk to one platform’s API
The company that hosts your app
quiz.why: Terraform itself knows nothing about AWS or GitHub; providers add that knowledge.

bridge.title: Where Terraform fits with Docker, Kubernetes, and Helm
bridge.description: Each tool in this course works on a different layer. Terraform usually builds the ground floor. Tool Its job Pizza example Terraform Create infrastructure:…
bridge.html:
Each tool in this course works on a different layer. Terraform usually builds the ground floor.

ToolIts jobPizza example
TerraformCreate infrastructure: networks, clusters, databases, DNS, permissionsMake the Kubernetes cluster, the database, and pizza.example.com
DockerPackage an app into an imageBuild pizza:v1
KubernetesRun and heal containers on a clusterKeep 3 copies of pizza:v1 running
HelmInstall an app’s Kubernetes files with chosen settingshelm install pizza ./pizza-chart
🧱 Terraform builds the cluster→🐳 Docker builds the image→☸️ Kubernetes runs it→⛵ Helm installs and upgrades it
The big idea
Terraform manages things that live a long time and change slowly. Your app changes every day; deploy it with Kubernetes and Helm, not by running Terraform for every release.

Terraform can also install Helm charts and Kubernetes objects through its Helm and Kubernetes providers. Many teams still keep the layers separate, so an app release cannot accidentally change the cluster underneath it.

Terraform creates and changes infrastructure. It is not the right tool for setting up the software inside a running server; build that into an image instead.
What about OpenTofu?

OpenTofu is an open-source fork of Terraform run by the Linux Foundation. Its files and commands are almost the same: type tofu instead of terraform. Everything in this course works with either.

Remember
  • Terraform builds the place; Docker, Kubernetes, and Helm run the app in it.
  • Keep slow-changing infrastructure and fast-changing app releases separate.

quiz.q: Which job is the best fit for Terraform?
options: Creating the Kubernetes cluster and its database
quiz.why: Terraform creates and changes infrastructure. Kubernetes heals containers; Docker builds images.

quiz.q: You release a new app version every day. What usually deploys it?
options: A new Terraform apply each time
quiz.why: App releases go through the deploy tools; Terraform changes the infrastructure underneath.

files.title: Read a configuration: blocks and resources
files.description: Terraform files end in.tf and use a language called HCL. All the.tf files in one folder are read together; that folder is called a module. Almost everything…
files.html:
Terraform files end in .tf and use a language called HCL. All the .tf files in one folder are read together; that folder is called a module.

The big idea
Almost everything is a block: a keyword, one or two labels, and settings in braces. A resource block says “make one of these, call it this, with these settings”.
resource "local_file" "menu" {    ← block type, resource type, your name for it
  filename = "out/menu.txt"       ← an argument: setting = value
  content  = random_pet.shop.id   ← a reference to another resource
}
BlockWhat it does
terraform { }Which Terraform version and which providers (with versions) this code needs
provider "aws" { }Settings for one provider, such as a region. Our example needs none.
resource "type" "name" { }Something Terraform creates and manages. Its address is type.name, for example local_file.menu.
data "type" "name" { }Reads something that already exists, without managing it.
variable, output, localsInputs, results, and named helper values (lesson 7).

References decide the order. Because the menu uses random_pet.shop.id, Terraform knows to create the shop name first. You rarely write the order yourself; Terraform draws a dependency graph from the references.

📄 main.tf · the course example
# Pizza Express learning project. Runs on your computer, no cloud account:
# - random_pet gives the shop a name
# - terraform_data stands in for a server (built into Terraform 1.4+)
# - local_file writes out/menu.txt, a real object you can open and break
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6.0"

  required_providers {
    local = {
      source  = "hashicorp/local"
      version = "~> 2.5"
    }
    random = {
      source  = "hashicorp/random"
      version = "~> 3.6"
    }
  }
}

locals {
  # A local names an expression once so several places can reuse it.
  menu_lines = [for pizza in var.pizzas : "- ${pizza}"]
}

# A new region means a new shop name: changing a keeper forces replacement (-/+).
resource "random_pet" "shop" {
  length = 2
  keepers = {
    region = var.region
  }
}

# Changing input updates this resource in place (~).
resource "terraform_data" "server" {
  input = {
    size   = var.size
    region = var.region
  }
}

# References to both resources above make Terraform create this one last.
resource "local_file" "menu" {
  filename        = "${path.module}/out/menu.txt"
  file_permission = "0644"
  content         = <<-EOT
    Shop:   ${random_pet.shop.id}
    Server: ${terraform_data.server.output.size} in ${terraform_data.server.output.region}
    Menu:
    ${join("\n", local.menu_lines)}
  EOT
}
Remember
  • A resource address is type.name, like local_file.menu.
  • References between resources decide the creation order.
  • All .tf files in one folder form one module.

quiz.q: What is the address of resource "random_pet" "shop"?
quiz.why: Type first, then your name.

quiz.q: The menu file uses random_pet.shop.id. What does Terraform do?
options: Creates the shop name first, then the file
Creates both at once in a random order
quiz.why: A reference is a dependency, so the referenced resource is created first.

workflow.title: init, plan, apply: the core loop
workflow.description: You wrote main.tf. Now what? Terraform never changes anything until you ask, and it always shows you its plan first. ✍️ write.tf → 📦 init → 🧾 plan → 👀…
workflow.html:
The problem
You wrote main.tf. Now what? Terraform never changes anything until you ask, and it always shows you its plan first.
✍️ write .tf→📦 init→🧾 plan→👀 you read it→✅ apply
CommandWhat it doesChanges real things?
terraform initDownloads providers into .terraform/ and records their exact versions in .terraform.lock.hcl. Run it once per folder, and again after adding providers or modules.No
terraform planReads the real resources, compares them with your code and the state file, and lists every change.No
terraform applyMakes the changes and records the results in the state file. Without a saved plan, it plans again and asks you to type yes.Yes
terraform destroyPlans to delete everything in the state file, then asks you.Yes
terraform init
terraform plan -out=tfplan   # save the exact plan you reviewed
terraform apply tfplan       # do exactly that plan, nothing else
The big idea
Saving the plan with -out and applying that file means Terraform does exactly what you reviewed, even if someone edits the code in between. If the state changed since you planned, Terraform rejects the stale plan.

Practice safely in the browser

Remember
  • init → plan → apply. Read every plan before applying.
  • plan never changes anything; apply does.
  • Commit .terraform.lock.hcl so everyone gets the same provider versions. Never commit .terraform/.

quiz.q: You cloned a teammate’s Terraform folder. What do you run first?
quiz.why: init installs the providers the code needs. Plan and apply come after.

quiz.q: Does terraform plan create anything?
options: Yes, a draft copy of each resource
No, it only shows what would change
quiz.why: Plan is a preview. Only apply or destroy change real resources.

state.title: The state file: Terraform’s memory
state.description: Terraform created a server. Next week you run plan again. How does it know that server is “its” server, and not something new to create? Terraform keeps a…
state.html:
The problem
Terraform created a server. Next week you run plan again. How does it know that server is “its” server, and not something new to create?
The big idea
Terraform keeps a state file, terraform.tfstate. It maps each resource address in your code to the real object it created, with that object’s ID and settings.
In your codeIn the state fileIn the real world
local_file.menuid = 3f2a…, filename = out/menu.txtThe actual file on disk
random_pet.shopid = clever-otterNothing: this resource only lives in state
terraform state list               # every address Terraform manages
terraform state show local_file.menu
terraform output                   # values from output blocks

Four rules for state

  • Never edit it by hand. Use terraform state commands or moved and import blocks instead.
  • Keep it private. State can contain passwords and keys in plain text. Never commit it to git.
  • Share it properly in a team. Store it in a remote backend with locking (lesson 12), so everyone uses one copy and two applies cannot run at once.
  • Back it up. Lose the state and Terraform forgets what it made; it would try to create everything again.
Think of it like…
A cloakroom ticket. The coat (the real resource) hangs in the back; the ticket (state) proves which coat is yours. Lose the ticket and getting your coat back is a lot of work.
Remember
  • State maps code addresses to real objects.
  • Never edit state by hand or commit it; keep it private and backed up.
  • Teams use a remote backend with locking.

quiz.q: You delete terraform.tfstate and run plan. What happens?
options: Nothing, Terraform reads the cloud instead
Terraform forgets what it made and plans to create everything again
quiz.why: Without state, existing objects are unknown to Terraform. Recovering means importing them back.

quiz.q: Should terraform.tfstate go into git?
options: Yes, so the team shares it
No: it can hold secrets, so use a remote backend
quiz.why: Remote backends share state safely and add locking.

vars.title: Variables, outputs, and locals
vars.description: Hard-coded values make code hard to reuse. Variables are the inputs, outputs are the results, and locals are named helpers inside. Terraform reads values in…
vars.html:
Hard-coded values make code hard to reuse. Variables are the inputs, outputs are the results, and locals are named helpers inside.

📄 variables.tf
variable "size" {
  description = "Server size. Changing it updates terraform_data.server in place."
  type        = string
  default     = "small"

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["small", "large"], var.size)
    error_message = "The size must be \"small\" or \"large\"."
  }
}

variable "region" {
  description = "Region. Changing it replaces random_pet.shop and rewrites the menu."
  type        = string
  default     = "eu-west"
}

variable "pizzas" {
  description = "Pizzas listed in out/menu.txt."
  type        = list(string)
  default     = ["Margherita", "Pepperoni"]
}
📄 terraform.tfvars
# Values here override the defaults in variables.tf.
size   = "small"
region = "eu-west"
pizzas = ["Margherita", "Pepperoni", "Funghi"]
📄 outputs.tf
output "shop_name" {
  description = "The generated shop name."
  value       = random_pet.shop.id
}

output "menu_file" {
  description = "The file Terraform manages."
  value       = local_file.menu.filename
}

Which value wins?

Terraform reads values in this order, and later ones win:

  1. The default in the variable block
  2. Environment variables such as TF_VAR_size=large
  3. terraform.tfvars, then any *.auto.tfvars files
  4. -var and -var-file on the command line
terraform plan -var size=large          # a one-off override
terraform plan -var-file=prod.tfvars    # a whole environment
The big idea
Variables let the same code build test and production with different values. Add a validation block so a typo fails at plan time instead of creating the wrong thing.
Mark passwords with sensitive = true. That hides them in plan output, but they are still stored in the state file in plain text. Protect the state.
Remember
  • variable = input, output = result, locals = named helper value.
  • Later sources win: default → TF_VAR_ → tfvars → -var.
  • sensitive hides values on screen, not in state.

quiz.q: The default is "small", terraform.tfvars says "large", and you plan with -var size=small. Which value is used?
quiz.why: Command-line -var is read last, so it wins.

quiz.q: Does sensitive = true keep a password out of the state file?
options: No, it only hides it on screen
quiz.why: State still contains it. Protect state like a secret.

plan.title: Read a plan: +, ~, -/+, -
plan.description: A plan says “1 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy”. Is that safe? It depends on what gets destroyed. Reading the symbols is the most important Terraform…
plan.html:
The problem
A plan says “1 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy”. Is that safe? It depends on what gets destroyed. Reading the symbols is the most important Terraform skill.
SymbolMeaningTypical cause
+CreateA new block in your code
~Update in place: the same object changesA bigger server size, a new tag
-/+Replace: destroy the old object, create a new oneA setting the platform cannot change on an existing object, such as the region
-DestroyYou removed the block from the code
The big idea
Look for -/+ and - first. Replacing a database or a disk can mean losing its data. Terraform marks the setting that causes it with “# forces replacement”.
  # server.web must be replaced
-/+ resource "pretend_server" "web" {
      ~ region = "eu-west" -> "us-east" # forces replacement
        size   = "large"
    }

Plan: 1 to add, 1 to change, 1 to destroy.

A replacement counts twice: one add and one destroy. Values Terraform cannot know until apply show as (known after apply); the DNS record’s new address is one, so the DNS record shows ~ too.

Practice safely in the browser

Protect important resources

Add lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } to a database so any plan that would destroy it fails. Use create_before_destroy = true when the new object must exist before the old one goes.

Remember
  • + create, ~ update in place, -/+ replace, - destroy.
  • Check every -/+ and - before approving: replacement can lose data.
  • prevent_destroy guards critical resources.

quiz.q: A plan shows -/+ on your database. What does it mean?
options: The database gets a small in-place change
The old database is destroyed and a new one is created
quiz.why: Replacement means a new object; data on the old one may be lost unless it is backed up.

quiz.q: One resource is replaced and nothing else changes. What does the summary say?
options: 1 to add, 0 to change, 1 to destroy
0 to add, 1 to change, 0 to destroy
quiz.why: A replacement is counted as one add and one destroy.

quiz.q: Which setting makes any plan that would destroy a resource fail?
quiz.why: It is a lifecycle safety catch for critical resources.

drift.title: Drift: when someone clicks in the console
drift.description: During an incident, a teammate makes the server bigger in the cloud website. It works. Nobody updates the code. Next week someone runs terraform apply……
drift.html:
The problem
During an incident, a teammate makes the server bigger in the cloud website. It works. Nobody updates the code. Next week someone runs terraform apply…
The big idea
Drift is any difference between the real world and what Terraform last recorded. Every plan reads the real objects first, so plan shows the drift and offers to put things back to match your code.

When you find drift you have two honest choices:

  • The code is right: apply, and Terraform undoes the manual change.
  • The manual change is right: edit the code to match, then plan until it says No changes.
terraform plan                  # shows the drift and the fix
terraform plan -refresh-only    # only update state to match reality
terraform apply -refresh-only

Adopt things that were made by hand

If a resource was created by hand and never managed by Terraform, add an import block and plan. Terraform adopts the existing object instead of creating a duplicate.

import {
  to = aws_s3_bucket.menu
  id = "pizza-menu"
}

Practice safely in the browser

The cure for drift is a habit: change infrastructure only through code and reviewed plans. Give most people read-only access to the cloud console.
Remember
  • Drift means reality differs from state; plan detects it.
  • Either apply to undo it, or update the code to keep it.
  • import blocks adopt existing resources.

quiz.q: Someone changed a server by hand. What does the next terraform plan show?
options: No changes, because Terraform only reads its state file
A change that puts the server back to match the code
quiz.why: Plan refreshes from the real world first, so it sees the drift.

quiz.q: The manual change was correct and should stay. What do you do?
options: Update the code to match, then plan
quiz.why: Make the code the truth again; plan should then say No changes.

quiz.q: A bucket was created by hand last year. How do you bring it under Terraform?
quiz.why: Import adopts the existing object into state.

modules.title: Modules: reuse without copy-paste
modules.description: You need the same setup (a server, a bucket, and DNS) for test, staging, and production. Copy-pasting it three times means fixing every bug three times. A…
modules.html:
The problem
You need the same setup (a server, a bucket, and DNS) for test, staging, and production. Copy-pasting it three times means fixing every bug three times.
The big idea
A module is a folder of .tf files: variables are its inputs and outputs are its results. Call it many times with different inputs. Every Terraform folder is already a module, called the root module.
module "shop_test" {
  source = "./modules/shop"   # a local folder
  size   = "small"
}

module "shop_prod" {
  source = "./modules/shop"
  size   = "large"
}

module "network" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"   # from the public registry
  version = "~> 5.0"                          # always pin registry versions
}

Read a module’s output with module.shop_prod.server_ip. After adding a module or changing its source, run terraform init again to download it.

Many copies inside one module

count = 3 makes three numbered copies. for_each makes one copy per item in a map or set, named by its key. Prefer for_each when items can be added or removed in the middle.

Think of it like…
A pizza recipe card. The card (the module) stays the same; each order (a module call) chooses its own size and toppings (the variables).
Remember
  • A module is a folder with inputs (variables) and outputs.
  • Pin registry module versions; run init after changing sources.
  • Prefer for_each over count when items can be removed.

quiz.q: What are a module’s inputs?
quiz.why: Variables are inputs; outputs are what callers can read.

quiz.q: You make three shops with count and remove the first one. What can happen?
options: The others shift position, so Terraform may replace them
quiz.why: count tracks items by position. for_each tracks them by key, so removing one leaves the others alone.

debug.title: When it goes wrong
debug.description: Most Terraform errors fall into a handful of patterns. Read the first error line, then find it here. You see Usually means First move Required plugins are…
debug.html:
Most Terraform errors fall into a handful of patterns. Read the first error line, then find it here.

You seeUsually meansFirst move
Required plugins are not installed, or Inconsistent dependency lock fileProviders are missing or changedterraform init (add -upgrade only on purpose)
Error acquiring the state lockAnother plan or apply is running, or one crashedWait and ask your team. Use terraform force-unlock ID only when you are sure nothing is running.
Resource already existsSomeone created it by hand, or state lost track of itAdopt it with an import block
No valid credential sources found, or 403The provider cannot log in to the platformCheck your cloud login and which account you are using
CycleTwo resources reference each otherBreak the loop; move one value into a variable or separate resource
Unsupported argument, or Invalid referenceA typo, or a setting from a different provider versionterraform validate, then the docs for your pinned version
terraform fmt         # tidy the formatting
terraform validate    # catch typos without calling the cloud
TF_LOG=DEBUG terraform plan 2> debug.log   # a very detailed log
The big idea
When an apply fails halfway, nothing is rolled back. Resources that succeeded are in state; the rest are not. Fix the cause and plan again: the plan shows only what is still missing.
Never delete the state file or run destroy to “start fresh” on shared infrastructure. Ask first.
Remember
  • Read the first error line; most errors match a known pattern.
  • After a partial failure, fix the cause and plan again.
  • force-unlock only when you are sure nothing else is running.

quiz.q: Plan fails with “Error acquiring the state lock”. What do you do first?
options: Check whether a teammate or CI job is running
quiz.why: The lock protects state from two writers. Force-unlock only after confirming nothing is running.

quiz.q: Apply created 2 of 3 resources, then failed. What is in state?
options: The 2 that succeeded; the next plan shows what is missing
quiz.why: Terraform does not roll back; it records what succeeded.

team.title: Teams: remote state, locking, and reviews
team.description: Two people run terraform apply at the same time from their laptops, each with their own state file. Now there are two servers and two different truths. In a…
team.html:
The problem
Two people run terraform apply at the same time from their laptops, each with their own state file. Now there are two servers and two different truths.
The big idea
In a team, state lives in one shared remote backend with locking, and changes go through review: open a pull request, let CI post the plan, approve, then apply from one place.
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "my-team-terraform-state"
    key          = "pizza/terraform.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true   # lock state while someone plans or applies
  }
}

Other backends include HCP Terraform, Azure Storage, and Google Cloud Storage. Move existing local state into a backend with terraform init -migrate-state.

A safe team workflow

🌿 branch→✍️ edit .tf→🤖 CI runs fmt, validate, plan→👀 review the plan→✅ merge→🚀 CI applies

Separate environments

Keep test and production in separate folders, each with its own backend, calling the same modules with different values. A mistake in test then cannot touch production. Terraform workspaces also exist, but separate folders make the difference easier to see in a review.

Never put secrets in .tf or .tfvars files in git. Read them at apply time from a secrets manager or environment variables, and remember they still end up in state.
Remember
  • One remote backend with locking per environment.
  • Changes go through pull requests with the plan attached.
  • Separate folders for test and production, sharing the same modules.

quiz.q: Why use a remote backend with locking?
options: So everyone shares one state and two applies cannot run at once
quiz.why: Shared state and locking prevent conflicting changes.

quiz.q: What should reviewers look at in a Terraform pull request?
options: The .tf changes and the plan they produce
quiz.why: The plan shows what will really happen, including replacements.

real.title: Run Terraform on your computer
real.description: Now use a real terminal. This project uses only your computer: no cloud account and no cost. Terraform will manage a generated shop name, a pretend server,…
real.html:
Now use a real terminal. This project uses only your computer: no cloud account and no cost. Terraform will manage a generated shop name, a pretend server, and a real file, out/menu.txt.

brew tap hashicorp/tap
brew install hashicorp/tap/terraform
terraform version

On Linux or Windows, use the official install page linked in the next lesson. OpenTofu works too: type tofu instead of terraform.

mkdir -p ~/terraform-pizza && cd ~/terraform-pizza
cat > main.tf <<'EOF'
# Pizza Express learning project. Runs on your computer, no cloud account:
# - random_pet gives the shop a name
# - terraform_data stands in for a server (built into Terraform 1.4+)
# - local_file writes out/menu.txt, a real object you can open and break
terraform {
  required_version = ">= 1.6.0"

  required_providers {
    local = {
      source  = "hashicorp/local"
      version = "~> 2.5"
    }
    random = {
      source  = "hashicorp/random"
      version = "~> 3.6"
    }
  }
}

locals {
  # A local names an expression once so several places can reuse it.
  menu_lines = [for pizza in var.pizzas : "- ${pizza}"]
}

# A new region means a new shop name: changing a keeper forces replacement (-/+).
resource "random_pet" "shop" {
  length = 2
  keepers = {
    region = var.region
  }
}

# Changing input updates this resource in place (~).
resource "terraform_data" "server" {
  input = {
    size   = var.size
    region = var.region
  }
}

# References to both resources above make Terraform create this one last.
resource "local_file" "menu" {
  filename        = "${path.module}/out/menu.txt"
  file_permission = "0644"
  content         = <<-EOT
    Shop:   ${random_pet.shop.id}
    Server: ${terraform_data.server.output.size} in ${terraform_data.server.output.region}
    Menu:
    ${join("\n", local.menu_lines)}
  EOT
}
EOF
cat > variables.tf <<'EOF'
variable "size" {
  description = "Server size. Changing it updates terraform_data.server in place."
  type        = string
  default     = "small"

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["small", "large"], var.size)
    error_message = "The size must be \"small\" or \"large\"."
  }
}

variable "region" {
  description = "Region. Changing it replaces random_pet.shop and rewrites the menu."
  type        = string
  default     = "eu-west"
}

variable "pizzas" {
  description = "Pizzas listed in out/menu.txt."
  type        = list(string)
  default     = ["Margherita", "Pepperoni"]
}
EOF
cat > outputs.tf <<'EOF'
output "shop_name" {
  description = "The generated shop name."
  value       = random_pet.shop.id
}

output "menu_file" {
  description = "The file Terraform manages."
  value       = local_file.menu.filename
}
EOF
cat > terraform.tfvars <<'EOF'
# Values here override the defaults in variables.tf.
size   = "small"
region = "eu-west"
pizzas = ["Margherita", "Pepperoni", "Funghi"]
EOF
terraform init
ls -a
head -n 12 .terraform.lock.hcl
terraform fmt
terraform validate
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform apply tfplan
cat out/menu.txt
terraform state list
terraform output

The plan should say 3 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy. After apply, open out/menu.txt in your editor.

sed -i.bak 's/^size .*/size   = "large"/' terraform.tfvars
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform apply tfplan

The server is updated in place. The menu file is replaced, because its content depends on the server’s output, which is only known after apply.

sed -i.bak 's/^region .*/region = "us-east"/' terraform.tfvars
terraform plan -out=tfplan
terraform apply tfplan
cat out/menu.txt

Expect 2 to add, 1 to change, 2 to destroy: a new shop name, a new menu file, and an in-place server change.

rm out/menu.txt
terraform plan
terraform apply

Plan shows + local_file.menu: Terraform noticed the file is gone. terraform apply without a saved plan shows the plan again and waits for you to type yes.

terraform destroy
terraform state list
ls out

The empty out/ folder, your .tf files, the lock file, and .terraform/ stay. Delete ~/terraform-pizza when you are done.

grad.html:
You are ready to use Terraform on a small project when you can complete these tasks without copying earlier commands.

Next project: set a billing alert first, then create one storage bucket with a cloud provider’s free tier, using a remote backend. After that, try creating a learning Kubernetes cluster with Terraform and installing the pizza chart on it with Helm.
